name: Robotic Grasping and Manipulation Competition
ability_definition: The ability to quickly move your hand, your hand together with your arm, or your two hands to grasp, manipulate, or assemble objects.

task_realism.reasoning: The Manufacturing Track uses a NIST task board with real industrial components. Tasks include peg insertion, gear meshing, electrical connector insertion, nut threading and disassembly/assembly. These closely mirror real assembly-line and bench-assembly work that exercises manual dexterity. It stops short of full realism because the board is a standardized test artifact, not an actual product with variable, compliant or partially occluded parts.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Execution is physical and timed, with a fixed time budget and a bonus for early completion. That captures the speed and reliability pressures of production work. However, the board layout is known in advance, CAD data is provided, and teams may design task-specific grippers and tooling. The 2020 remote format further controlled the setting. Real workplaces bring more part variability, clutter, changeover and unforeseen perturbations, so the conditions are more structured than most real work.

construct_coverage.reasoning: It covers the core elements of the ability: grasping, manipulation and assembly, with explicit rewards for both completion and speed. The coverage is still a slice, though. It uses one board with a limited set of mostly rigid, small parts. Bimanual coordination is not specifically required, deformable-object handling is limited, and novel objects are absent. Custom grippers can also let a team solve the specific board rather than demonstrate general dexterity.

format_match.reasoning: The inputs are real physical parts and fixtures, and the output is a physically assembled or disassembled board scored on completion and time. This matches real work artifacts and performance metrics far better than simulated success rates or abstract formats. A points-per-subtask scheme on a test board is still slightly artificial compared with producing a finished product to quality specifications.

transferability_reasoning: The competition tests physical, timed grasping and assembly of real industrial parts, a strong match for the speed-and-assembly nature of Manual Dexterity. Transfer is limited by the highly structured, pre-known task board, the allowance of CAD data and task-specific grippers, and a narrow set of mostly rigid parts. Together these mean success may reflect board-specific engineering more than general, adaptable dexterity.

2020.model_or_system: Team SDU (University of Southern Denmark) autonomous assembly workstation
2020.metric: competition points (273 task points maximum, plus a time bonus)
2020.human_reference: Median manufacturing assembly worker or typical adult doing hand assembly of small mechanical and electrical parts (pegs, gears, connectors, nuts)
